rows.Finding / value: J. Jayalalithaa; also Jayaram Jayalalithaa, Jayalalitha and Jaya. Born 24 February 1948; died 5 December 2016. “Amma” is a political honorific, not a formal office.

rows.Finding / value: Rajya Sabha member, April 1984–January 1989; Assembly member from several constituencies; twice Leader of Opposition; dominant AIADMK leader and Chief Minister across six ministries.

rows.Finding / value: The official Assembly list records six ministries beginning in 1991, 2001, 2002, 2011, 2015 and 2016. The last two were consecutive. The 2001 appointment was judicially invalidated.
rows.Corroboration: See field evidence; independent origins are identified in Sources.

rows.Finding / value: Nine Assembly constituency contests are recorded: eight wins and the 1996 Bargur defeat. The two 1991 victories count separately as contests. The 2001 rejected nominations are not polling defeats.
rows.Corroboration: See field evidence; independent origins are identified in Sources.

rows.Finding / value: Cradle Baby Scheme, Amma canteens, drug procurement and rainwater-harvesting requirements provide distinct policy mechanisms. Their existence does not establish sole personal responsibility for statewide social gains.

rows.Finding / value: Vision 2023 set infrastructure and growth ambitions. The workbook treats those as plans and targets, with implementation and independent outcome assessment still incomplete.

rows.Finding / value: Her government defended the existing 69% reservation arrangement; Parliament supplied Ninth-Schedule protection. Water litigation and Sri Lankan Tamil demands show state-level pressure on wider institutions.

rows.Finding / value: Cinema-derived recognition, centralised party authority, changing alliances and the maternal “Amma” identity combined with visible benefits. These mechanisms require separate evidence, rather than one personality-based explanation.

rows.Finding / value: First woman Leader of Opposition in Tamil Nadu, but not its first woman Chief Minister: Janaki preceded her. A 2016 survey found stronger AIADMK support among women; that is not proof of gender equality within the party.

rows.Finding / value: TANSI acquittal coexists with judicial criticism of conflicts of interest. The 2014 assets conviction and 2015 acquittal preceded the 2017 judgment: appeals against her abated on death; surviving co-accused were convicted.

rows.Finding / value: Mass employee dismissals, contested welfare spending and the 2015 floods raise distinct legal, fiscal and administrative questions. None should be collapsed into an undifferentiated corruption label.

rows.Finding / value: Electoral resilience and durable welfare institutions coexist with criticism of concentrated authority and inadequate succession. Supportive and critical assessments are attributed on the Legacy sheet.

claims.statement: J. Jayalalithaa; also Jayaram Jayalalithaa, Jayalalitha and Jaya. Born 24 February 1948; died 5 December 2016. “Amma” is a political honorific, not a formal office.
claims.review_note: Common aliases identify the subject. No separate legal-name certificate was inspected.

claims.statement: Born in the Mysore region, educated in Bengaluru and Chennai, and prominent in cinema before entering Tamil Nadu politics. Exact birth locality remains unresolved.
Joined AIADMK in 1982. MGR’s mentorship helped entry; the succession struggle after his death required her to establish a separate organisational and electoral claim.
Rajya Sabha member, April 1984–January 1989; Assembly member from several constituencies; twice Leader of Opposition; dominant AIADMK leader and Chief Minister across six ministries.
The official Assembly list records six ministries beginning in 1991, 2001, 2002, 2011, 2015 and 2016. The last two were consecutive. The 2001 appointment was judicially invalidated.
Nine Assembly constituency contests are recorded: eight wins and the 1996 Bargur defeat. The two 1991 victories count separately as contests. The 2001 rejected nominations are not polling defeats.

Cradle Baby Scheme, Amma canteens, drug procurement and rainwater-harvesting requirements provide distinct policy mechanisms. Their existence does not establish sole personal responsibility for statewide social gains.
Vision 2023 set infrastructure and growth ambitions. The workbook treats those as plans and targets, with implementation and independent outcome assessment still incomplete.

Her government defended the existing 69% reservation arrangement; Parliament supplied Ninth-Schedule protection. Water litigation and Sri Lankan Tamil demands show state-level pressure on wider institutions.

Cinema-derived recognition, centralised party authority, changing alliances and the maternal “Amma” identity combined with visible benefits. These mechanisms require separate evidence, rather than one personality-based explanation.

First woman Leader of Opposition in Tamil Nadu, but not its first woman Chief Minister: Janaki preceded her. A 2016 survey found stronger AIADMK support among women; that is not proof of gender equality within the party.

TANSI acquittal coexists with judicial criticism of conflicts of interest. The 2014 assets conviction and 2015 acquittal preceded the 2017 judgment: appeals against her abated on death; surviving co-accused were convicted.
Mass employee dismissals, contested welfare spending and the 2015 floods raise distinct legal, fiscal and administrative questions. None should be collapsed into an undifferentiated corruption label.

Electoral resilience and durable welfare institutions coexist with criticism of concentrated authority and inadequate succession. Supportive and critical assessments are attributed on the Legacy sheet.

Public recognition and MGR’s patronage created access; campaigning and succession conflict show that celebrity did not automatically supply authority.
Editorial interpretation links Tamil identity, social justice and welfare to her political claims despite a background different from the movement’s dominant anti-Brahmin tradition.
“Amma” personalised state provision through a protective maternal image; survey evidence of women’s support is a separate empirical question.
Journalistic assessments describe intense loyalty and limited internal dissent. They criticise the shortage of an independent second rank; this is interpretation, not a party-wide survey.
Withdrawal of support in 1999 illustrates regional-party leverage in a coalition at the Centre; her demands did not confer constitutional authority to appoint a Union government.
The 2013 Balaji judgment records competitive distribution promises by both DMK and AIADMK; institutional incentives extended beyond one leader.
Water litigation used courts; Sri Lankan Tamil resolutions pressed the Union. Legal relief and political demand are distinct instruments.
2016 survey analysis reports stronger female support across several demographic groups. It cautions against treating welfare or leadership credibility alone as a complete explanation.
Violence is documented; the specific allegation that her sari was pulled is disputed by DMK and later witnesses.

She challenged conviction and secured High Court acquittal during life. Death prevented final appellate relief against her.

Research lead: inquiry findings and competing medical report; later disposition unverified

A 2002 restriction and 2004 announced reversal raise questions about minority rights and policy consistency.
Legal and political controversy; repeal chain unreviewed
Reported government rationale was religious harmony; reversal was presented as responsiveness to minority concerns.
Eight wins across nine constituency contests, judicial interruptions and the 2016 return distinguish personal popularity from uninterrupted incumbency.
Canteen institutions and procurement systems offer observable legacies; delivery, institutional survival and effects on welfare require different measures.
Survey evidence of women’s support strengthens the account of political identification. It does not establish that all women shared interests or gained equivalent organisational authority.
TANSI ethical criticism, the invalidated 2001 appointment and the assets-case disposition demand legal precision alongside electoral assessment.
Indian Express’s editorial credits hard-won authority while criticising personality-centred leadership and lack of a strong second rank.
Srinivasan and Bedi see a continuing role for surrender-based protection while warning about weak follow-up and the underlying devaluation of daughters.
Vision 2023 broadens the record beyond subsidies, but its numerical ambitions cannot be substituted for an audited record of achievement.
The 1989 clash and the posthumous inquiry show how political memory remains disputed. Later repetition cannot substitute for original records or adjudication.

Cinema and MGR mentorship opened access; campaigning and succession conflict were additional steps to leadership. Editorial accounts identify patriarchal barriers, without measuring their separate causal weight.
First woman opposition leader in 1989. Janaki’s 1988 chief-ministership rules out calling Jayalalithaa the state’s first woman CM.
MGR’s patronage, Janaki’s family-based succession claim and Jayalalithaa’s own campaigning supplied different pathways. Sasikala’s later influence requires separate scrutiny from recruitment.
She attained broad chief-ministerial power, rather than being confined to a welfare role. The collected material does not establish how gender shaped allocation of portfolios to other women.
An editorial explicitly interprets her career through patriarchal cinema and political institutions. A matched sample of media treatment of male and female rivals has not been assembled.
The 1989 Assembly violence and her specific disrobing allegation had gendered political meaning; the allegation’s details remain contested. No comprehensive threat/security record was collected.
Cradle protection, women’s canteen employment and marriage-assistance rules provide substantive policy pathways. They do not by themselves establish improved autonomy or equality.
The maternal “Amma” image connected leadership with provision. It is an attributed strategy of representation, not evidence that voters lacked agency.
2016 post-poll analysis found a female voting advantage for AIADMK. Descriptive leadership, voter identification and redistribution are distinct from women’s authority within the party.
Contemporary electoral analysis, the 2010 cradle study and later recollections of 1989 produce different kinds of assessment. None should become a timeless empowerment or victimhood label.
Political entry occurred within MGR-led AIADMK; his death exposed a disputed succession rather than an automatically inherited office.
Rajya Sabha membership gave an institutional platform before Assembly leadership. State executive power and party position were separate routes.
1984 entry was an indirect parliamentary election; it must not be counted as a constituency popular-vote victory.
No inspected period study isolates how the changing economy affected her childhood, film work or early political choices.
No inspected evidence establishes a decisive international-system influence on her early choices. Later Sri Lankan positions must not be projected backwards.
Cinema visibility preceded party rallies and campaigning during MGR’s illness. Later television and digital assumptions cannot be applied to this entire phase.
Propaganda work and MGR’s patronage supplied organisational access; the later split demonstrates limits to uncontested authority.
Sources describe a Brahmin background and a female cinema-to-politics pathway within Dravidian politics. Identity alone does not explain party recruitment or voter acceptance.
Movement between Mysore, Bengaluru and Chennai preceded a Tamil Nadu political career. Historical birthplace and later constituency are different geographies.
Commemorative biographies compress offices and retrospective reporting contains chronology errors. Precise office registers and Tamil-language archives remain priorities.
Leadership was consolidated through competition with the Janaki faction and DMK; first government followed the 1991 victory, then personal defeat in 1996.
Opposition leadership, Assembly confrontation and reservation legislation show the importance of legislative and Union institutions, alongside executive power.
Won Bodinayakkanur in 1989 and two seats in 1991, then lost Bargur in 1996. Seat-level records must remain separate from statewide mandate.
Welfare and procurement institutions expanded. A period-specific analysis linking liberalisation, state finances and her policy choices is not yet collected.
A source-based account of how the post-Cold War and Sri Lankan conflict settings affected the first government remains incomplete.
The 1989 clash circulated through news reporting and later political memory. Contemporary reports and later witnesses differ over specific actions.
Her post-MGR leadership became increasingly centralised in journalistic accounts, while networks around Sasikala drew scrutiny.
Female-infanticide concern and reservation politics identify distinct gender and caste-policy pressures; neither policy alone measures equality.
Bargur and Kangayam victories show multiple electoral bases. Parliament’s role in quota protection demonstrates Centre-state interdependence.
Original election PDFs could not be read; secondary tables preserve counts with known transcription defects. Long-term policy evaluation requires other evidence.
Regional-party leverage in the national coalition is directly visible in the 1999 withdrawal; state office resumed in 2001 and again in 2002.
Courts invalidated the 2001 appointment, sustained TANSI acquittal and considered mass employee dismissals: majority support did not remove institutional constraints.
Rejected 2001 nominations differ from the 2002 by-election win and 2006 Assembly victory. Legislative office and chief-ministerial appointment followed different rules.
Drought-related harvesting requirements and employee-strike policy illustrate resource and labour choices. A comparable fiscal series remains uncollected.
The current evidence does not map her positions across the Sri Lankan war and global economic changes in this entire period.
Contemporary coalition reporting and later water-policy reporting provide different evidence windows. A systematic television/campaign archive has not been inspected.
Party influence survived disqualification and absence from executive office. Coalition withdrawal and the subsequent electoral return show distinct uses of organisational authority.
The employee conflict and the revived cradle programme affected different constituencies. Neither identifies a uniform social response to her government.
Andipatti supplied a legislative base; Delhi coalition bargaining operated beyond state borders. The 2006 victory did not itself mean retention of government.
Judicial texts offer strong procedural evidence, while by-election reports disagree on totals. Review of legal holdings does not validate every reported political motive.
Returned in 2011 and retained government in 2016; DMK remained a major rival. Vote distribution, alliances and gendered support complicate a single-cause explanation.
Assets litigation interrupted office; welfare litigation and interstate-water adjudication separately constrained government action.
Srirangam in 2011 and RK Nagar in 2015–16 were distinct contests. The 2015 opposition boycott limits comparison of margins and shares.
Vision 2023 combined infrastructure ambitions with a welfare-expansion period. Planned growth and the cost or effectiveness of benefits require independent evaluation.
Postwar Sri Lankan Tamil claims entered state politics through the 2013 resolution; implementation depended on Union and international institutions.
Video-conference canteen openings and personalised scheme branding linked administration and public communication. Digital-campaign effects are not measured here.
The Amma identity personalised party leadership and public provision. Editorial criticism of a weak second rank is an attributed institutional assessment.
Post-poll research found stronger female support across several groups; urban flood exposure and region also shaped reporting on the result.
Canteens operated through municipal institutions; water litigation joined two states. Neither statewide leadership nor local delivery was institutionally self-contained.
Born-digital plans, court judgments and surveys are relatively accessible; failed official links and limited posthumous inquiry access still constrain reconstruction.
